title: CCTV Upgrade and Privacy Rules

opening.text: The CCTV upgrade is funded across the region. The vendor wants to demo face recognition and 'behaviour analytics' to the committee on Thursday, and HR tells me the staff are nervous about cameras in the back of house. Can you get ahead of both? Marguerite.

briefing: 10:00, Tuesday. A regional CCTV upgrade is funded: new cameras, recorders and a central system. The vendor is pushing analytics; staff are worried about being watched.

Veldane CCTV rules: every camera has a stated purpose (safety, security, evidence) and is no more intrusive than the purpose needs; never in guest rooms, toilets, changing or locker rooms or rest areas; signs where cameras operate; no audio; 30-day retention unless footage is kept for an incident; access only by trained, named users, logged; footage released only through a written request process; a privacy impact assessment and counsel's review before any new use, including analytics; staff consulted before back-of-house changes. Local law decides the details. Your authority is 3,000,000.

context.text: Counsel still has the profiling complaint from the trafficking poster on file. Anything that sorts people by how they look will be scrutinised.

learningObjectives: A purpose for every camera, and the places cameras never go
Analytics only after a privacy impact assessment and counsel

actions.label: Survey the camera plan against the rules
actions.finding: The vendor's plan adds 140 cameras across the region. Each is checked for a purpose: most are sound (doors, cash points, docks, lift lobbies, car parks). Problems: two cameras in the staff locker room 'for theft', one facing the staff smoking shelter with audio, and a lift-lobby camera on 14 that looks straight into 1412 when the door is open.

actions.label: Approve the locker room cameras to stop locker thefts
actions.finding: The cameras go into the locker room where staff change. Within days the union and HR have a formal complaint, and the footage itself is now a liability.

schedules.description: Staff take the locker room cameras to the data protection regulator. The hotel is ordered to remove them and fined; the press covers it.

actions.label: Consult the staff on the back-of-house cameras with HR
actions.finding: With Priyanka and the staff forum: the plan is shown camera by camera. The locker room and audio cameras are dropped; the locker thefts are dealt with by better locks and a key log instead. Staff ask who can see the footage and why; the answer goes in the policy.

lines.speaker: hr_director
lines.text: People don't object to cameras on the dock. They object to not knowing who's watching and why. Tell them, and most of this goes away.

actions.label: Hear the vendor's analytics pitch with counsel's questions
actions.finding: The demo: face recognition against a 'banned guests' list, and 'suspicious behaviour' alerts. Counsel's questions: what is the legal basis, how accurate is it for different people, who is on the list and how do they get off it, what happens on a false match? Nobody can answer. The committee agrees: no face recognition; any analytics only after a privacy impact assessment, counsel's sign-off and a pilot.

lines.speaker: gm
lines.text: If we can't explain to a guest why the camera stopped him, we don't switch it on.

actions.label: Switch on face recognition in the lobby for the banned list
actions.finding: The system flags three 'matches' on the first evening. One is a banned guest; two are not, and one is stopped at the lift in front of his children. He asks under what authority the hotel scanned his face.

schedules.description: The guest wrongly stopped by face recognition complains to the regulator and the press. The system is switched off by order.

actions.label: Re-aim the floor 14 lift-lobby camera away from the room doors
actions.finding: The camera is moved to cover the lift doors and the stair door, with a privacy mask over the room doorways. It still shows who comes and goes on the floor.

actions.label: Set the access, retention and release rules with Ines
actions.finding: Named, trained users only; every view and export logged; 30 days then overwritten unless an incident hold is placed; footage released to police, insurers or claimants only on a written request, approved by LP and counsel, with the custody log. Ines points out the old recorder allowed a shared login: the new one won't.

lines.speaker: partner
lines.text: One login per person, every export logged. After Vessey, I'm not sharing a password again.

actions.label: Agree the signs at every camera zone
actions.finding: Signs at every entrance and camera zone: that CCTV operates, why, who runs it and how to ask about it. The guest privacy notice and staff handbook say the same.

actions.label: Issue the regional CCTV policy
actions.finding: Camera register with a purpose for each; the places cameras never go; no audio; signs; retention and incident holds; named access and audit logs; the release process; the privacy impact assessment required before any new use; an annual review with HR and counsel.

options.label: Guest rooms, and views into them
The loading dock
options.feedback: The dock is exactly where a camera has a clear security purpose.

questions.prompt: The vendor offers face recognition for banned guests. What do you recommend?

options.label: Not without a legal basis, a privacy impact assessment, counsel's sign-off and evidence it is accurate and fair; for now, no.
options.feedback: Biometric surveillance of every guest is a high bar. If you can't meet it, a trained eye and a good photo do the job.

options.label: Switch it on: it only flags people already banned.
options.feedback: It scans everyone's face to find the few, and it makes mistakes. A false match is a guest wrongly stopped.

options.label: Trial it quietly in the lobby first.
options.feedback: A quiet trial is still scanning every guest without telling them.

questions.prompt: An insurer emails asking for last week's lobby footage. What happens?

options.label: A written request with the reason, approved by LP and counsel, exported with the custody log, only the relevant clip.
options.feedback: Footage is personal data. Every release has a reason, an approval and a record.

options.label: Send them the whole day: they're our insurer.
options.feedback: Only what the request needs, and only through the process.

options.label: Refuse: footage never leaves the hotel.
options.feedback: Lawful, justified requests are part of what the cameras are for.

options.label: 140 cameras checked for purpose; locker room and audio cameras dropped after staff consultation; floor 14 camera masked; no face recognition, analytics only after PIA and counsel; named access, logs, 30-day retention and a release process.
options.feedback: What was installed, what wasn't and why, and the rules that govern it.

options.label: New cameras and analytics installed across the region.
options.feedback: Analytics weren't installed, and the rules are the point.

options.label: Staff objections delayed the upgrade.
options.feedback: Staff consultation removed two cameras that should never have been planned.

checks.label: A purpose for every camera
checks.pass: Every planned camera was checked for its purpose.
checks.fail: The vendor's plan went in unchecked.

checks.label: Not where people change
checks.pass: No camera went where people change.
checks.fail: Cameras went into the locker room.

checks.label: No face recognition
checks.pass: Nobody's face was scanned without a basis.
checks.fail: Face recognition went live without an assessment.

checks.label: Consult the staff
checks.pass: Staff were consulted before the policy was issued.
checks.fail: Staff heard about the cameras from the installers.

checks.label: Access and release
checks.pass: Named access, logs, retention and a release process.
checks.fail: Anyone can view and export footage.

checks.label: No view into rooms
checks.pass: The floor 14 camera no longer sees into rooms.
checks.fail: A camera still looks into a guest room.

checks.label: Tell people
checks.pass: Guests and staff can see where cameras operate and why.
checks.fail: Nobody is told about the cameras.

checks.label: Issue the policy
checks.pass: The regional policy is issued and reviewed yearly.
checks.fail: The rules exist only in your head.

debrief.whatHappened: You took a funded CCTV upgrade and made it lawful and trusted: a purpose for every camera, none where people change, no audio, a masked view on floor 14, no face recognition without an assessment, staff consulted, and clear rules for who sees footage, how long it's kept and how it is released.
bestPractice: A stated purpose for every camera; no more intrusive than it needs.
Never in rooms, toilets, changing or rest areas; no audio.
Named access, logged; 30-day retention; incident holds.
Release only on a written, approved request with custody.
A privacy impact assessment and counsel before any new use, analytics included.
debrief.why: Cameras protect people only while people trust them. Every camera in the wrong place, and every face scanned without reason, spends that trust and invites the regulator.
commonMistakes: Switching on analytics because the vendor can.

lesson: Purpose for every camera, never where people change, no analytics without assessment, access and release rules.
